extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating Markush claim groupings and statutory patentability conditions (novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 and non‑obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103). Primarily written for examiners conducting claim examination, with content useful to applicants and counsel drafting or responding to rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush grouping propriety (primary test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is proper if the alternatives defined by the Markush group share a “single structural similarity” and a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two situations meet this requirement: (1) the alternatives are all members of the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art‑recognized class and are disclosed in the specification or known in the art to be functionally equivalent and have a common use; (2) where the Markush grouping describes alternative chemical compounds that do not belong to a recognized class, the members may be considered to share a single structural similarity and common use if they share a substantial structural feature that is essential to a common use and the common use flows from that substantial structural feature. See MPEP §2117 and cited cases (Harnisch, Hozumi, In re Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single structural similarity — recognized class criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Members share a 'single structural similarity' when they belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art‑recognized class (i.e., the art expects members will behave similarly in the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: each member could be substituted for another with the expectation of achieving the same intended result. Example: various fasteners for a disposable diaper may be an art‑recognized class because prior art shows substitutability to achieve repositionable/refastenable function. Note: existence of such a recognized class can tend to prove equivalence and, if one member is anticipated, may render the group unpatentable absent convincing evidence of non‑equivalency (In re Ruff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single structural similarity — substantial structural feature for chemical compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When alternatives are chemical compounds not in a recognized class, they may still be proper if they share a substantial structural feature essential to a common use, and the use flows from that feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claimed compounds as wholes (do not break down into elements of substituents). Example: coumarin core common to dyes (Harnisch) or phosphoric acid diester backbone with common antimycotic activity (Hozumi). The structural feature must be substantial and disclosed as essential to the utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative lens: treat claimed compounds as wholes
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining propriety of a Markush grouping, each compound must be considered as a whole and not broken down into elements or components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid focusing only on the variable moiety defined by Markush language; instead examine whether the overall molecules share the required substantial structural similarity and common use. Decisions are fact‑specific and case‑by‑case (Harnisch, In re Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping — examiner rejection procedure (Form Paragraph 8.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: When species do not share a single structural similarity or a common use, reject the claim as containing an improper Markush grouping using Form Paragraph 8.40.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph language should be used; bracketed insertions must be completed (bracket 1: claim numbers; bracket 2: description of the Markush group; bracket 3: explanation why the alternatives fail the two prongs). Explain why alternatives are not in a recognized class and/or not functionally equivalent, and/or why they do not share a substantial structural feature and associated common use. Note: if an election of species requirement is appropriate, use this form only after applicant has made an election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions to applicant for overcoming improper Markush rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should suggest how applicant may overcome an improper Markush grouping rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: suggest a proper Markush grouping based on the specification, or suggest that applicant present each alternative (or grouping of patentably indistinct alternatives) in a series of independent or dependent claims. Do not suggest any grouping that clearly would not meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or would clearly lack adequate written description if presented in a separate claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of improper Markush grouping rejection and election of species practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on an improper Markush grouping should be made in the first action on the merits after presentation of the claim with the improper grouping; examiners should also require an election of species for search and examination if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the improper grouping rejection in the first Office action on the merits (or next Office action following presentation). If a written provisional election of species must be made separate from the first Office action on the merits, that provisional election should not include an improper Markush grouping rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of a Markush claim because they cannot envision all of the members, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 112(b) when a boundary cannot be drawn separating embodiments encompassed by the claim from those that are not. See also MPEP §2173.05(h). This rejection is in addition to any improper Markush grouping rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining, overcoming, and reconsidering improper Markush grouping rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until the claim is amended to include only members that share a single structural similarity and a common use, or the applicant presents convincing arguments that the members do share these features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant fails to overcome the rejection, maintain it. However, when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance, the examiner should reconsider the propriety of the rejection and withdraw it if, in light of the prior art and record, the alternatives do in fact share a single structural similarity and common use. No Markush claim may be allowed until improper grouping is overcome or withdrawn and all other conditions of patentability are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case‑by‑case determination — illustrative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Propriety of Markush groupings is fact‑specific and must be decided case‑by‑case; MPEP provides examples (Harnisch, Dams, Hozumi, PCT Example 33) showing proper and improper groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided examples to inform analyses (e.g., Harnisch treated coumarin core as substantial feature producing dye utility; PCT Example 33 showed mixed herbicides from disparate chemical classes lacking a substantial shared structural feature). The examples emphasize treating compounds as wholes and examining disclosed utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Definition of novelty/prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, or was described in an issued patent or published application effectively filed before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP quotes statutory language and editor notes applicability to AIA vs pre‑AIA filings. This is the baseline novelty/prior art standard examiners apply when assessing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — One‑year grace period exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date is not prior art if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly/indirectly from the inventor, or (B) the subject matter had previously been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a person who obtained it from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these exceptions when analyzing whether a pre‑filing disclosure constitutes prior art for applications subject to the AIA; consult the statute for precise conditions and timing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Exceptions for disclosures in patents/applications and common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure in a patent or application is not prior art under subsection (a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained from the inventor; (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor before the patent/application was effectively filed; or (C) the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these exceptions and consider the common ownership provision, including the related joint research agreement conditions: (1) subject matter developed by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date, (2) invention made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement, and (3) patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties to the joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — Effective filing date of patents and published applications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: For determining whether a patent or application is prior art under subsection (a)(2), the effective filing date is the actual filing date, or if entitled to priority/benefit under listed sections, the earliest such application's filing date that describes the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether an issued patent or published application is prior art, determine whether the patent/application claims benefit/priority to earlier filings; use the earliest effective filing date for subject matter described therein as the relevant prior art date.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — Obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability under 103 is assessed by considering whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a PHOSITA. The manner in which the invention was made does not negate patentability. The MPEP also cites statutory variations (pre‑AIA language) and special biotechnological process provisions (see subsection regarding composition/process claims owned by same person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology/process‑composition exception under 35 U.S.C. 103(b) (pre-AIA phrasing included)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under subsection (b) (editor note: applicable language for certain filings), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel and nonobvious may be considered nonobvious if claims to the process and composition are contained in the same application or separate applications having the same effective filing date, and both were owned by the same person at the time invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions are met, a patent issued on a process must also contain claims to the composition of matter used or made by that process. This statutory carve‑out modifies obviousness analysis for biotech process/composition claim sets and includes ownership/assignment conditions.
